vignette: Juan Hernandez still recalls the sound of shattering glass and the crunch of metal on pavement. It was a typical Friday evening when his nephew, Alex, had been stopped by police for a minor traffic infraction. What followed was a chaotic scene that would forever change Juan's life. The officers, seemingly agitated, dragged Alex out of the car, pinning him to the ground. Juan, who had arrived at the scene moments earlier, watched in horror as his nephew's face was pressed into the asphalt, blood streaming from his nose and mouth. In the aftermath, Juan became consumed by images of Alex's battered face and the haunting memory of his own powerlessness. He couldn't shake the feeling that he should have done more to intervene. As time passed, these memories began to surface in unexpected ways. Whenever Juan saw someone with visible injuries or wounds, his mind would instantly flash back to that fateful night. He found himself steering clear of hospitals and medical dramas on television, unable to bear the sight of others' suffering. As a tax consultant, Juan's work required him to meet clients at various locations across the city. However, since the incident, he'd become increasingly anxious about visiting unfamiliar places, always wondering if danger lurked around every corner. He'd begun to restrict his travel, opting for familiar routes and avoiding new neighborhoods altogether. When out in public, Juan frequently glanced over his shoulder, checking to see if anyone was following him – a habit that had started to feel like second nature. Even simple tasks, like going to the grocery store, became a source of anxiety as Juan meticulously planned escape routes before entering the premises. His clients began to notice changes in his demeanor, and some even commented on his increased irritability. Despite this, Juan couldn't shake off the feeling that he needed to be constantly vigilant. Physical pain also served as a trigger, transporting Juan back to the scene of Alex's beating. Whenever he experienced a headache or muscle ache, his mind would conjure up images of Alex writhing in agony on the ground. These episodes left Juan reeling, questioning whether there was something inherently wrong with him that had contributed to the traumatic event. Juan's feelings of isolation deepened as he withdrew from social interactions and stopped attending family gatherings. He couldn't help but wonder if his life was still worth living, now that the trauma had seemingly consumed every waking moment. The weight of these thoughts bore down on him, making it increasingly difficult to find meaning in his work or relationships. As Juan's world shrunk further, he became convinced that there must be something fundamentally flawed about himself – a notion that tormented him day and night. His sense of self-worth was battered, much like Alex had been on that fateful evening. Now, after months of struggling to come to terms with the past, Juan finally sought help, hoping to break free from the grip of these haunting memories and find some semblance of peace. It was the realization that he couldn't continue living in a state of constant hypervigilance, always expecting the worst, that brought Juan to therapy. He feared losing himself entirely to the trauma, but he also clung to the hope that, with time and guidance, he might rediscover a sense of purpose and learn to live alongside his memories rather than being controlled by them.
